subtopic: PROMOTION OF SEASONAL EMPLOYEES
PROMOTION OF SEASONAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
1.	Is it the policy of the civil service commission to promote seasonal employees who are employed for specified periods under section 51 of the Civil Service Act in periods when such employees are not employed?
2.	If so, is such a policy consistently followed in all competitions involving such classes of employees?
3.	If not, when and under what conditions are such promotions made?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROMOTION OF SEASONAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I have been given the following answer by the civil service commission:
1.	Where it is considered that qualified candidates might be found among seasonal

employees, it is the policy to admit such employees to competitions regardless of whether the competition is or is not held during a period in which they are required to perform their duties. A seasonal candidate, who was the successful candidate could be promoted during the period in which he was not required to perform his duties, as well as during the season in which he was employed, but the promotion in either case would be effective only from the date on which he assumed his new duties.
2.	Yes.
3.	Not applicable.
Note: The wording of the first part of the question has been discussed with Mr. Bell and it has been established that section 51 of the Civil Service Act is not applicable in the context of this question.

Answer: (a) and (b). Data are not available in the form requested. subsubtopic: POSITION OF CANADIANS HELD AS HOSTAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Can he give the house any information regarding the three Canadians who are allegedly being held as hostages by certain elements of the population in Bolivia?

subtopic: BOLIVIA
subsubtopic: POSITION OF CANADIANS HELD AS HOSTAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to this question I may say that the British ambassador in Bolivia, with whom we have been in close touch, Canada not having a mission there, has confirmed the news reported by the press that a number of persons, including three Canadians and four United States citizens, have been forcibly detained by striking miners in Bolivia. Both the press and the ambassador have identified two of the Canadians as Raymond Brousseau and Aurele Falar-deaux, both presumed to be from Kirkland Lake, Ontario. The name of James McNamee of Kingston, Ontario, has also been given in the press but this has not yet been confirmed by the British ambassador. Although it is not certain, there was a report from the British ambassador that Robert Morrison of Ottawa was detained, but a later report now says that he has been released.
It appears that some but not necessarily all of the 21 persons detained by the miners are being held as hostages in order to secure the release by the Bolivian government of two trade union leaders. We have asked the British ambassador to call again on the Bolivian government with instructions to make strong representations to that government to ensure the safety and the release of the Canadians.
Our ambassador in Peru, who is also accredited to Bolivia, is going to La Paz tomorrow morning, the earliest time he can reach that city, and he will of course do everything possible to help the Canadians who have been detained.

This is a job which is carried out in many departments and is necessary to the proper administration of the department in providing information to the various media, as well as conducting other office routine on behalf of the minister. It is a function which is carried out in all ministers' offices. speechtext: I simply ask the minister this. Can he point to one example, under the British parliamentary system, where a serving officer becomes an interpreter for a minister?

subtopic: POLICY STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES

subtopic: POLICY STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think if you will examine the evidence given before this special committee on defence by the chiefs of the three services, you will find that there are rare occasions when there was any interference in respect of answering questions, and then only when they related to matters of unresolved government policy when the minister, who has the responsibility, took over the questions.

subtopic: POLICY STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Would the minister agree that the functions of such an officer are certainly not to announce any reductions in expenditures, which ought to be done by the minister in this house?

subtopic: POLICY STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Quite so; and none was, I can assure you.

subtopic: POLICY STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: I have a further question to the Minister of National Defence. I wonder if the minister could inform the house whether Group Captain Lee is paid by the government, by the air force, or by the minister? subtopic: POLICY STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I object to this question, to the manner in which it was put forward. Group Captain Lee is paid by the Royal Canadian Air Force and his pay, like the pay of all other personnel, civilian or service, in the department, comes out of departmental appropriations. I might say, for my hon. friend's benefit, that this is not a precedent. The previous minister of national defence had a special assistant, Lieutenant Colonel Christian, who was seconded to the minister's office. There have also been precedents for serving officers making statements. When the previous administration was in office Vice Admiral Brock went on television to explain certain developments, and I think it should be set clear nothing we have done in recent times is in any way a precedent which is not in accordance with parliamentary principles and practices.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: LONDON, ONT.    REPORTED REDUCTION IN PAY OF SEASONAL HELP
speechtext:
I have an urgent question for the Postmaster General. I understand from representations made to me that the casual Christmas employees at the London post office have had their pay reduced from $1.43 to $1 per hour in the middle of their eight weeks of special employment. Would the Postmaster General inform me if this reduction in pay is general in all post offices in Canada, or just in this isolated instance?

Inquiries of the Ministry [Translation]

subtopic: LONDON, ONT.    REPORTED REDUCTION IN PAY OF SEASONAL HELP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for telling me beforehand that he would ask that question.
In reply, I must say that temporary employees hired during the holidays in urban offices in Canada are paid as follows: sorting helper, $1 per hour; mailman's helper, $1.25 per hour; mail handling helper, $1.25 per hour. All other occasional help is still getting $1.43 per hour.
It may happen that some people work occasionally to replace regular employees who are absent and that their employment is terminated when the regular employees come back to work. If those people are subsequently hired to help during the Christmas season, they are paid according to the wage schedule I have just given.

As far as the London employees referred to by the hon. member are concerned, the postmaster at London informs the department that seven persons who were employed as casuals at $1.43 per hour in November, replacing absent employees, were released because the absent employees returned to duty, and these seven people have now been offered re-employment as Christmas helpers at $1 per hour.

subtopic: LONDON, ONT.    REPORTED REDUCTION IN PAY OF SEASONAL HELP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a very definite question of the Postmaster General because of the month we are now in, and I speak from experience of almost 30 years in opposition, 10 of them in this house. They can also write to the Postmaster General himself who will refer the names to the respective post offices. There are so many ways that I think the hon. member can rely on any one of them to recommend applicants.

And even if we raised the question of privilege in that regard, the problem I am referring to-and the Secretary of State is well aware of what I mean-has not yet been settled to our satisfaction. Therefore, I ask the Secretary of State to look into that matter at the same time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-124, to amend the Gold Mining Assistance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps the house will not expect too much of an explanation this afternoon on this amending bill, because on November 27 as we were coming to the end of the session I took the precaution of explaining to the house the purposes of this bill.
The bill amends the assistance that has been available to gold mines since 1948. In brief there are only two matters of substance or change in the amending bill. One is that the assistance will continue for a term of four years. This is the longest term that has ever been offered in an amending bill. The other matter is the reference in the statement I made, as reported at page 5144 of Hansard, respecting a denial in about 18 months hence of assistance to new gold mines, where employees would not normally evolve around an existing community that was dependant upon the gold mining economy.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION AND MAKING CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the minister for the brevity of his statement, because I expected he might have gone into

further detail in regard to his bill, particularly in regard to some of its new provisions. The minister's statement of November 27 was welcomed by the gold mining communities inasmuch as it removed any doubts as to the possibility of the gold mining industry not relying on the assistance which they had been getting, particularly since 1958, at an increased rate. Since the coming into force of the emergency provisions I believe a total sum of close to $170 million had been paid up to the end of 1962. That assistance not only contributed but I think in most cases enabled the gold mines to remain in operation and produce for Canada the metal which is a source of great wealth. It also contributed in a very striking way to the prosperity of large sectors of our country.
I would have liked the minister to give the house some explanation about the restrictions which would apply to new mines after July 1, 1965. That particular provision has been questioned with anxiety by the gold mining communities and also by prospectors generally throughout this country. It could, I think, lead to a curtailment of the operations of a very vital industry for Canada, and I am afraid it will have a dampening influence on prospectors and mineral exploration. It may foreshadow within a few years a notable decrease in the amount of assistance which the government will be giving to the gold producers.
The main reason this provision has given rise to anxiety is that in its application it may defeat a most laudable objective, namely an extension of gold mining activities to other areas throughout Canada. Surely this country has not reached the stage where it feels it has a sufficient supply of gold. There is a saying which the minister must often have heard; "Gold is where you find it". Does this provision mean that if in the future a new discovery of substantial proportions is made outside the established gold mining communities, and a mine is established it will not qualify for assistance? If that is so I think the mining people are justified in viewing the provision with great alarm.
I was surprised that the minister did not amplify his statement in this respect this afternoon, and I hope he will do so before the end of the debate, because this is an important matter. I do not think this is the sort of measure which should be whipped through without adequate scrutiny. There is, I feel, something abnormal in the fact that the government must give emergency assistance to an industry which has contributed so much to the wealth of this country and which is producing a metal that is sought throughout the world. Throughout the centuries gold has been the one product which
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has always been in demand. It could always fetch its price. Yet despite this, and despite the fact that there is a world shortage of the metal, the gold mining industry has to be treated as a depressed industry requiring emergency treatment.
Of course we know the reason for this situation. It is because there has not been an increase in the price of gold since 1933, at which time the price of gold was raised from $20.62 an ounce to its present price of $35 in United States currency. Since that year, despite mounting costs and inflation throughout the world and despite the ever increasing demand for gold, the price has remained unchanged. This has been one cause of high prices in many countries and of a decline in activity, not merely in mining activity but economic activity generally. To my mind this measure, welcome as it is in its principles, and necessary as it is to the degree that it provides assistance to the gold producers is still nothing but a palliative, nothing but a stopgap.
It would seem according to informed observers, people in financial circles and experts who have made a special study of gold and its price, that the real solution to the problems of the mining industry and also, perhaps, to the slackening in the economies of several of the leading industrial nations of the world, would be an increase in the price of gold. There is a very good case to be made out in favour of such an increase at this time. One reason is that there exists a world shortage of the metal. Supplies of gold, including annual production, are insufficient to look after the normal needs of trade and commerce, and insufficient to accommodate public purposes.
To give the house an example, let me point out that in 1962 the combined governments of the western world were able to purchase only $325 mililon worth of gold out of a fresh supply of some $1,550 million. Most of the supplies which were purchased by the governments of the western world went to meet the normal demands of trade and commerce. A much larger share went into the hands of hoarders and speculators who for several years made a practice of accumulating gold in the belief that soon the world price will have to be increased.
The supply is short in Canada and it is short in the United States. As a matter of fact, in 1962 the United States had to earmark some $12 billion of its supply of gold simply to back up the United States dollar, which left only about $3 billion for normal interchange. In addition, it must be remembered that foreign demands on United States currency amount to some $15 billion and, of course, if all those demands were required
5602	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to be met in gold, as they have a right to be met if the creditors insist, the United States gold stock would be almost entirely depleted.
There have been potent reasons why the United States should resist the world wide demand for an increase in the price of gold. To accept it would be tantamount to a devaluation of the United States currency. Nevertheless the advantages to be derived from an increase in the price of gold are obvious. There would be an immense stimulation of trade and industry. Unemployment would be reduced. More aid could be given to underdeveloped countries.

speechtext:
Why did you not do it
when you were in office?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION AND MAKING CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I will give an example, one which might at the same time answer the very intelligent observation just made by the Secretary of State. His interventions are always intelligent. They are always in the interests of shortening our debates and getting his legislation passed more smoothly. I take this occasion to congratulate him on his subtlety.
In any event, the Secretary of State asked me why this was not done while we were in office. In doing that he displayed an astonishing amount of ignorance, because a decision of that kind does not depend on the Canadian government. It makes no difference which party is in office; it is not the province of the Canadian government to increase the world price of gold. That can only be done by the power which controls the international market for gold and which controls the price on an international scale, that is the United States government. I am sure the Secretary of State knows that very well. But last year, in 1962-since the Secretary of State did bring this matter up, and because it is pertinent to the debate-the Canadian government of that day did devalue the Canadian dollar by a small amount, to 92J cents in relation to the United States dollar. We know that this devaluation has already had, and will continue to have, as the figures for foreign trade reveal, a stimulating effect on the Canadian economy. It benefited Canada's foreign exchange position and, of course, resulted in an increase in our trade earnings.
Similar benefits, but on a much larger scale, would derive from an increase in the price of gold to say double its present price, making it $70 U.S. an ounce, which would amount to a devaluation of United States currency by half. An increase in the price of gold, the advantages of which I have just outlined, would help most industrial countries


in the world but they would help Canada in a very particular manner because Canada is one of the primary gold producing countries of the world. The latest gold production figures I have are for 1961 although the minister may have the 1962 figures; but I would point out that in 1961 production of gold amounted to 4,425,000 ounces. Canada, of course, is a developing country with vast potential mineral reserves still untapped. There is no doubt that, as occurred in 1933 and later after the world price of gold was increased, a great new wave of mining exploration would follow today if the world price were increased. This would result in new gold discoveries which would help to alleviate the world shortage of gold and would bring new prosperity to Canada and create new communities where today only wilderness exists.
Not only the gold mines would benefit from the new mineral exploration and prospecting, which would be sparked in this way, but there would also be discoveries of other minerals, thereby enhancing Canada's position as one of the leading countries of the world in mineral production. In turn, secondary industries and the economy in general would greatly benefit from such a move.
Most people who have studied the situation are in agreement in saying that this is the one single action that could contribute most to Canada's prosperity. Perhaps I might give an example of the contribution one single mine can make to the economy of the country. Let me take Dome Mines Limited of South Porcupine, northern Ontario, which is not far removed from my own constituency. In 1961, this mine bought supplies from 126 communities in Canada broken down in this way: 82 in Ontario, 22 in Quebec, 9 in New Brunswick, 6 in Nova Scotia, 2 in Saskatchewan, 2 in Alberta, 2 in British Columbia and 2 in Manitoba. These purchases were made from a total of 622 companies. This means that in addition to the very worth-while contribution arising from the production of gold by this mine, gold being in great demand, as I have said, the benefits from the operation of this one gold mine are spread out in an intricate network throughout the entire country.
In my own constituency we had a notable gold producer which ceased operations a few years ago, not because it could not survive financially but because the reserves had been depleted. I am referring to Belle-terre (Quebec) Gold Mines Limited. My constituency has along one border and on its fringe the pre-Cambrian shield which extends through northwestern Quebec and northern Ontario and in which are found the

majority of Canada's gold producers. I often wonder what would have happened to our country during the dark and deepest days of the depression if it had not been for this vigorous industry which provided employment for so many people and also provided an impetus, encouragement and inspiration to the rest of the country which at that time was stagnating under the severity of a world-wide depression.
Because of the reasons I have just mentioned I believe the time has come for the government to initiate talks with the United States government and perhaps also with the world monetary fund officials in order to have the situation fully examined and to reach conclusions that might influence the United States government to decide to take the imperative step of increasing the price of gold. As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, we are happy that the legislation is being extended but we hope it will not result in the initiation of a policy on the part of the government that will lead to the discouragement of mineral exploration, because if that were to happen it would be a very sad day for the industry, for the mining communities and for the country as a whole. I am looking forward to further explanations from the minister when he closes the debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION AND MAKING CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very happy to have the opportunity again to support the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and its extension for another four years. We do this knowing that the minister must be having certain difficulties with his conscience because of not having made the act permanent rather than emergency legislation. I think all who are interested in gold mining will agree that the industry is not likely to go ahead under present circumstances but that gold production is very apt to become a dying field of endeavour, and therefore the emergency that was apparent 17 years ago will still be apparent until the last one of the gold mines closes down.
We are very sympathetic to the position the minister takes in stipulating in the new legislation that assistance will not be provided to new areas developing gold production if it results in the establishment of new communities, but rather for the development of producers in areas already dependant on gold mining.
I believe the minister is to be congratulated on having learned one lesson which the Canadian people learned at considerable expense in the case of Elliot Lake where assistance was given to the development of a new
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act mining field and the creation of a town without making sure that the industry would continue to be able to exist over a period of years.
I agree with something that the last speaker said but I would point out that he had the opportunity and failed to do anything about changing the price of gold. It is very easy for me to say this is a worth-while endeavour and that the price of gold should be increased, because I think this would solve the problems of many of the producers in my area and would have a favourable reaction so far as many of the producers in other areas are concerned. However, we are all aware of the fact that Canada as a prime producer of gold is dependant upon the international monetary fund, and more particularly the United States, for the price of the product.
I might give an example of something that happened years ago when I was a miner, and the president of a union that was on strike and had been for a number of years. I visited the president of this small independent company for which I worked. The company owned three gold mines. I went to the United States to discuss the matter of settling the strike with the president. I thought that the company I had worked for was quite a sizeable one but I was very impressed by the fact that while he was the president of the company he was also considered, in the United States city in which he lived, to be the largest real estate holder in that area. In addition, he was the head of one of the largest legal firms in that city and had many other interests besides gold mining.
The only reason I was able to see him was that I was naive enough to think that I should be able to do so. When I arrived in his office I told his receptionist that I wanted to see the president, giving his name. She asked me if I had an appointment and I said no. She said, "Who will I tell him is asking for an appointment?" I gave her my name and I said, "You can tell him I work for him in Timmins". When she told him that he decided he had better find out whom he was employing in Timmins, because I imagine he never considered any of us in the gold mining field to be his employees.
We discussed the matter of increasing the price of gold, and it is not quite as simple as the miners or some of the mines sometimes think. He said to me, "I have a little money tied up in gold mines and I should like to see the price of gold go up but if the price of gold goes up you can easily figure out what this is going to mean to me in dollars and cents in relation to my real estate". It is easy for us to think only that Canada is in the
5604	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act position of producing gold, and we are not really too interested in the stockholders. The stockholder, of course, has to make a profit or he is not going to be interested in the particular field, but over a period of years the stockholders have made sizeable profits from many of the existing mines. The contribution made to the nation has been dealt with by the previous speaker. It is a contribution that cannot be overemphasized. It is not generally known that there are many other industries in Canada dependant upon the gold mining industry in one way or another. It is interesting to ride on the trains and, in talking to the engineers, learn that during the depression they worked for the gold mines under some sort of hoisting licence, and then were able to go back to the running trade after the depression. The same thing is true in so far as the manufacture of cable and other supplies is concerned.
There is much more gold, I am sure, under the pre-Cambrian shield than has been mined. It is necessary, in my opinion, for the Canadian government to go to the international monetary fund and demand an increase in the price of gold. We really cannot separate gold from the other monetized metals, but I think the time has come for Canada to decide whether or not we are getting proper value for the gold we export at $35 an ounce, or whether the Canadian government should stockpile it. We have never really objected to the mines stockpiling gold, and I want to talk about that later in connection with McIntyre. One time they were mad at the government and they stockpiled gold.
We have said many times that they are using this scheme to low-grade their property. This is a matter of great concern to the miners who are dependant on that ore. However, that is not the purpose of my intervention today. First of all, I believe the minister should remove the word "emergency" from this measure. We would be quite happy to move an amendment when we reach the committee stage, because I think the minister will agree that unless something happens we do not foresee at the moment, there is really no possibility at the end of four years of not having to extend this legislation.
I think we have an obligation to the communities because the communities have been literally unable to do anything for themselves. Not long ago the representatives of these communities came to Ottawa and, at the invitation of the minister, I sat in on the presentation of the briefs by the representatives of these communities. I should like to quote one sentence from one of the briefs. In the conclusion, the brief refers to the fact that the mines in these communities have derived $170 million in aid over the past


16 years. They want this continued because they have not been able to arrive at any other solution. The brief reads as follows:
Beyond this immediate question, however, we have tried to persuade you and your colleagues and fellow members, that the time is opportune for an imaginative reappraisal of the whole scope and purpose of the legislation as an instrument of national economic development.
As an aside, I would say that I am sure this could be revised in many ways. However, I presume the only way they want it revised is upward. However, the brief reads as follows:
Economic growth is the core of much of your policy thinking these days, just as it was of ours in, for example, the 1958 study of the gold mining community. Diversification has proved to be a rocky road to economic growth in the gold towns, until already the areas around Timmins, Val d'Or, and Rouyn-Noranda have been defined by your government as being so depressed as to be eligible for special federal assistance in business development. Most of the gold mining communities are in equal difficulty. Considering the gamut of local, national and international considerations bound up in gold mining, we would conclude this submission by calling to your attention the tremendous impetus to economic growth which would flow from a truly positive approach to the extraction of our gold resources.
Well, there is a difference of opinion even amongst the representatives who came to Ottawa. I am happy to say that my area may be just a little more progressive, a little more advanced in its thinking, than they are in Porcupine and some other areas. This is true for a very simple reason which does not relate to a difference in people or a difference in areas. The only difference is that many of the gold mines in Kirkland Lake have closed down, and those that have not closed are in the process of informing their shareholders and everyone in general that they are on the verge of closing down. The problem in this area, therefore, is immediate so far as the producers are concerned. They have made other suggestions which I believe the government is considering. I hope the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidickson) will keep in touch with the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) because it is my opinion that this money we are paying out in the form of emergency gold mining assistance would be better paid for the development of secondary industry. If we are going to take care of the transition period, I would say that the $17 million we will be paying this year could be better used in the development of secondary industry.
We have been interested in some of the things that have happened. One of the most interesting developments has been that of the McIntyre mine, which has adopted an archaic attitude toward some of its companies. This company may talk about the

earnings of employees over the years, but at the same time they do not say much of what has been paid to shareholders or what the company, as an entity, has earned. The company has undertaken some development, but that has not any relationship to the amount of money the company has taken from the emergency gold mining assistance fund. The nearly quarter of a million dollars which has flowed from the fund to this company, in my opinion, has not been in keeping with the amount of profit the company has earned.
I suggest we should be interested in this matter. In 1962 we gave McIntyre $1,064,000 in aid. Then, that year McIntyre had a profit of $5,330,760 on which they paid income tax of only $67,586. I suggest that this is a cause for some alarm when we know that some of the smaller producers in adjacent areas are paying half of their total profit in income tax. As an example I cite the case of Cisco in the Gowganda area, a silver producing mine. I want to compare these two mines for the benefit of hon. members. In 1962, Cisco had a profit of $469,000, a little less than half a million dollars, on which they paid income taxes of $224,000, almost a quarter of a million dollars. McIntyre made $5.5 million of profit and yet only paid $67,586 in income tax. I think there is a great disparity between the two which we should think about.
The people of the community are of the opinion that the department has not the facilities to really ascertain upon what the emergency gold mining assistance is being paid at McIntyre. I have a statement here, and I will read some of it. It is to be found in sessional paper 88A of November 1962. We have in the Gowganda area a silver producing mine called Castle, which in 1958 was made a division of McIntyre mines. This mine has been making a very large profit and, according to the figures, has been paying about half a million dollars or so to McIntyre each year. We are of the opinion that the greater the loss at Castle, the more E.G.M.A. will be earned because costs have risen at McIntyre. This is not a separate branch, it is a division of McIntyre itself. If you make a calculation of the E.G.M.A. that has been paid to McIntyre, you will find a sizeable increase each year since Castle was made a division of McIntyre.
Why should we be interested, one way or the other? One of the reasons is that McIntyre has been living in the dark ages so far as their employees are concerned. The gold mining industry has paid the lowest wages of any mining industry in Canada. I think, Mr. Speaker, you would be interested in this, that the gold mines paid the lowest
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act wages; silver paid a better wage, as did copper, zinc and the other base metals. The highest wage in the mining industry accrued to the iron miners, the lowest base metal we have in the mining industry. It looks to be the case that the higher the price of the product, the more precious the metal, then the lower are the wages in the industry. There is a definite relationship all up the scale.
The silver mining industry has been organized for some time. The two mines in Gowganda were organized last year by the united steel workers, and Siscoe made an arrangement in keeping with the wages in the silver mining industry. The Castle, owned by McIntyre, is run by an old mining baron by the name of Campbell, who for many years has had a connection with the Castle mine and who is an engineer with McIntyre. He has always kept his finger on the pulse of the gold mining area at Castle, but since the contracts were not agreeable the Castle closed down. This has meant that the McIntyre is showing a loss of $500,000, which will probably be made up by increased amounts under E.G.M.A., which means that the E.G.M.A. payments will be higher in 1964 because the Castle closed its operations.
I do not know if we can bring any pressure on this company to divorce itself from the wing of McIntyre, so that the miners can be re-employed, but we are going to make it really miserable for McIntyre until they allow the only silver company in my area to meet with the employees and make some arrangements.
The former minister got himself involved in this matter of surveys, but mining is a very difficult proposition. I laid a charge one time on information that was given to me regarding a particular stope at the McIntyre, which was one of these high grading stopes. The department said they would investigate it and report the findings of their investigation. However, according to my information, this investigation was never made, and it is also my information that if they are going to do this surveying they will have to borrow the men from the provincial department of mines because there are very few people in the department who can go underground and do the physical work involved.
Here is a letter sent out on February 28, 1962, from the head of the taxation and legislation section of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, to Mr. P. B. Mc-Crodan, manager, McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited, Schumacher:
Dear Sir:
T. W. Verity and W. J. Beard inspection engineers, will visit your mining property on or about March
5606	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act 23, 1962 to carry out duties in connection with the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act with respect to the designated year 1961.
Would you kindly prepare certain relevant information and plans prior to the visit. A "List of Data" and a copy of an inspection report form are attached for your guidance and convenience in the preparation of the information.
Yours truly,
E. C. Hodgson Head,
Taxation and Legislation Section.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I worked for a long time in the mines and one of the greatest complaints miners had was the fact that in Ontario, when a safety check was going to be made at a mine, the mine was phoned up and told on Friday night about the check. Finally, because of our complaints, the government realized this was not a fair process, because all the men were taken off the work they were doing and were put to work making the mine safe so that the inspector would not get himself killed when he walked through it.
The department finally quit notifying the mines, but the inspectors came up with a different gimmick. An inspector would visit a mine the day before, bring his clothes and hang them in the dryer, which very fact indicated he was going to do the inspection there next day before he went anywhere else. We do not believe in this kind of inspection.
I mention the McIntyre in this connection, because not only have they played around with silver but they are now concerned with a new copper project. They have been fortunate enough to develop a copper body by accident. They were doing development work for gold in a gold mining area, and fortunately found themselves with a very large low-grade copper project close to their gold workings. I suggest that these mining inspectors were not, in 1962, able to do an evaluation for 1961 of the costs of production in that mine because they were not in a position to take into consideration the cost division between the development in copper and the development in gold.
We know that in 1963 the mine is ready to go into production. Now, we want to be very fair to the department because they have had requests to operate this as a separate mine, but after hearing briefs on the subject they have decided it is not a separate mine, and they are not going to allow the three year tax period from the development. I note that on September 9, 1963 they wrote to McIntyre Porcupine Mines as follows:
In examining the application submitted by your company for assistance for the period January 1 to June 30, 1963 it has been noted that a deduction of costs applicable to the copper mine has been made from the costs of producing gold listed on


the ''General expenses at mine" sheet. This together with a number of items showing increases in costs has raised the problem of providing a suitable means for the examination of the division of costs made between the production from the McIntyre gold mining unit and the McIntyre copper mining unit.
Would you be good enough, in the third quarter application for 1963 and subsequent applications, to submit detailed information on the cost of production from the copper mining unit in a manner similar to that used in the presentation of the cost of production of gold through the use of sheets number 1, 2, 3, 4A, 4B, and 5, schedule II.
The application for the second quarter of 1963 has been approved for advance payment in the amount of $210,495.25. In arriving at the amount of advance due, a holdback rate of 25 per cent was applied in view of the possible changes in the division of costs between copper and gold. Your attention is also drawn to an error in subtraction in the amount of $100,000 which was made in the computation of the amount of advance due in the application as submitted.
It was very nice that they should draw this small matter of $100,000 to the attention of the mine. I did not think McIntyre had that kind of accounting system and would make that kind of mistake. But, Mr. Speaker, you will see this is causing a great deal of concern. My concern is not so much in presenting difficulties to McIntyre in getting E.G.M.A., but in the fact that I think they are damned crooks so far as their employees are concerned. If they do not straighten up their affairs with their employees, then we shall be after them because the employees really are the communities. The employees working in these mines provide their communities with all the taxes they need for municipal services. The mines pay very little taxes and buy a very small amount of their materials locally, mostly on a wholesale level, so that it is the wages of the people they employ which provide the lifeline for the communities.
If McIntyre start playing around with their employees they are going to be in trouble with me, with the E.G.M.A. inspectors, and I am sure with the minister. Our avowed purpose in supporting E.G.M.A. is not that it is a cure-all for keeping life in these communities, but that it is a stopgap measure to keep the communities in existence until we can arrive at a system of providing them with industrial assistance as an alternative to gold mining.
So long as Canada is not interested in handling gold as an export commodity, and treating it as a mint commodity which the government itself is going to sell, then we are not interested in mining gold. We do not care if we have gold in our stockpiles because we do not use it as backing for money. It is the same as if Ford were manufacturing cars in Canada and were exporting them to

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
the United States at a set price, and the reason the set price is there is the reason we are supporting E.G.M.A. assistance to these communities.
Therefore, we are giving advance notice that we are going to war on McIntyre until they decide they are going to do something about their employees. This company has several hundreds of millions of dollars in its portfolio, to invest in various forms across the nation, and every red cent of it was built up on the money it earned on the work, labour and resources that the Canadian people has had in the gold mining industry in the Porcupine area. The company has an obligation, because the miners are only earning $1.25 an hour, and they are working underground for that low wage. The base wage in most of the iron mines is well over $2 an hour. There are sweepers getting close to $2 an hour in the base metal industry. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are not asking for anything extra and certainly nothing in keeping with the occupation in which they work and the hazards under which they work. We are not asking for anything more than is due to the communities that were built around them. We are pleased, therefore-despite what I say about McIntyre-to support E.G.M.A. We think the controls being exercised by the department are probably not strong enough or active enough, however, to curtail a company that is perhaps out to beat the department.
This government is anxious, no doubt, as other governments have been, to keep the industry alive with this emergency gold mining assistance. I am not sure in my own mind that McIntyre has not abused the purpose of this act. To illustrate the attitude of these people I should like to read this letter. This is a letter that goes in to the department quarterly, four times a year. It is from McIntyre Porcupine Mines, Limited and says:
We enclose herewith, in quadruplicate, application of this company for the six months period ended June 30th, 1961 for assistance under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
Will you please give this claim your usual prompt attention and forward your cheque for $308,268.09 at your early convenience.
In other words, "Get cracking; my money is due". People do not write like this when their pension cheque is overdue. This is the attitude they use to the communities, to the government and to everybody with whom they deal. When they go to arbitration they speak of the master and servant arrangement; they go back to laws that have long been repealed. Therefore we think there has to be much closer supervision of a company that appears to be increasing over the years with the assistance of E.G.M.A. and which we find is in a position to make over $5 million profit.
I think a legitimate question to ask is, why should we be making a donation of $1 million to this company, when the profit they are making is so considerable? If they can prove this is for the production of gold and there are other factors involved, I think this is perfectly all right. But I suggest that when this copper project goes into operation we will have the same difficulty with the new product, with regard to getting better wages out of this company, because they will continue to use gold as the reason for not paying decent wages, instituting any pension plan or doing anything for the community or the people.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister, and I hope all hon. members will support the idea of not allowing new gold mines to develop outside those areas where gold is already a major production factor. This means, as I understand it-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that if new mines can be found in Matachewan, Kirkland Lake or Timmins, these gold mines will be supported under the same type of arrangement-

speechtext: With a proper margin of profit.

Yes, of course, taking into consideration the cost of production and other factors. But we hope this will not be extended into new gold mining areas if such were found on the outskirts of Ottawa or somewhere else, and particularly in areas more remote, for the simple reason that we want this matter of emergency gold mining assistance to produce benefit and assist the welfare of the gold mining communities as long as those communities are dependant on this industry as their source of income.
We also ask the minister to give complete co-operation to the Minister of Industry in searching out, through surveys and whatever means are available, all possible avenues for developing secondary industry in these areas so that sooner or later these communities will find themselves again in the self-supporting position which they desire, and which 1 think the Canadian people desire for them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the basis that the better you know your subject, the shorter your speech will be, I can say that I know the gold subject very well. However that is not exactly the case and I shall be very brief in my comments. I do wish to go on record as supporting the extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, because we believe it is essential for our gold mining industry in Canada at the present time.
5608	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
The world situation in regard to the supply of gold is rather critical. For over 20 years now, in fact for almost 30 years, the price of gold has been at a fixed rate. The cost of living in all parts of the world has increased rapidly during this period of time, but the price of gold has not increased. From one aspect this has caused a great deal of pressure upon the gold market of the world, and it is becoming obvious that the price of gold will have to be increased in the not too distant future if this commodity is to continue to form the basis of international exchange, as it does at the present time.
There is no doubt that on an international basis we are in trouble with the gold standard, even as we were in trouble with the gold standard on an internal basis in 1935. This situation is forcing a new policy to develop in regard to international settlements. However, until this comes about I think the gold market will continue to be very strong as far as the need of the world for more gold is concerned. Certainly in Canada we should be doing all we can to increase, rather than decrease, the amount of gold produced. In other words, because of the short demand on gold today the demand for gold will continue for some time, even though the previous speaker mentioned that gold in its relative importance as a trading commodity may eventually go out of the picture altogether.
This brings me back to the point that it is important that the E.G.M.A. policy be continued, and we support the government in extending it at this time. I am particularly grateful to the minister for including in this extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act new mines which might come into existence within the next 18 months; that is, up to June 30, 1965. This means that new mines in the process of being developed at the present time are protected as well as mines which are actually in production. This is not the place to debate this matter at the present time, but I believe it is important that the government restudy and reassess its entire policy of taking care of the gold mining situation. I believe that the inevitable developments which will take place within our own economy as far as gold is concerned and also internationally, as far as the use of gold is concerned, demand that some more satisfactory policy be worked out to cover the gold mining industry. In the meantime there is no alternative but to extend the present policy, which is being done in this piece of legislation.
I do not wish to belabour the point any further, Mr. Speaker, but I repeat that we give our support to this bill. At the same time we urge the government to initiate immediately a study of how our over-all gold


policy can be improved upon. We support the provision that new mines coming into operation in the next 18 months will also be covered by this assistance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION AND MAKING CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
it is too late in the day and too late in the season to take up too much time on the bill before us today. However there are a few things I should like to say. I wonder whether the government has really come to grips with this problem of gold, or whether they have just sort of swept it under the rug for another four years. After all, if we look back over the history of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act we see that it goes back some 16 years now. I would like to know from the government just what has been solved in those 16 years. Are we any closer to a solution of the problems of the gold mining industry today than we were 16 years ago, in 1948, when this act was first passed? Furthermore, over those 16 years has the government really done any housekeeping on this act? Have they given an appropriate accounting of their stewardship in regard to the $175 million or $180 million of the taxpayers' money that has been spent in this industry?
I was rather shocked two or three years ago when the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and myself dug into this matter and we found that over the years money had been paid out and there was not even an inspector on the payroll of the federal government to inspect these mines and see whether the money paid by the government was in fact being earned by the industry.
Like Caesar's wife, the industry was beyond suspicion and its word was accepted for everything. That has not been the experience of the gold miners who have worked for this industry over the years. It has not been the experience of the gold mining communities which have been dependant on this industry. These companies are not the knights in shining armour that we might think them to be, when we consider that the federal government is paying hundreds of millions of dollars into an industry without making arrangements for proper supervision and inspection to see how this money is being used.
My hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has pointed out that the wages paid in the gold mining industry are still the lowest paid in any mining industry in Canada. I think this is something the government should think about, as it pays out this money over the years. I think responsibility rests on the shoulders of this government to make a closer check on this industry than has been made in the past. My hon.

Emergency Cold Mining Assistance Act
friend from Timiskaming also mentioned the subject of safety. I think the records will show that gold mining is as dangerous an industry as any in the country today.
There is another aspect of this question to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) might turn her attention. I was asked, rather jokingly, by some people in Toronto at one time whether everyone in the Porcupine area was on the provincial welfare payroll. I admit that a great many are. The percentage of those in the gold mining areas who have to fall back on the welfare arrangements of the provinces and the municipalities is probably higher than it is elsewhere. This, I say, is a direct result of the neglect shown by an industry which is shirking its responsibilities and shifting them on to the shoulders of the municipal taxpayers who, in turn, are the employees of the industry. I have in my files many hundreds of cases of men who have been injured or who have lost their health working in the gold mines. They have been shed by the industry like old clothing and they have had no choice but to fall back on the municipality for assistance. I think this is a scandalous state of affairs; it is a situation which the federal government should look into before it opens the purse strings to subsidize this industry for another four years.
I think, too, that the government should look back over the 16 years during which this act has been in operation. I believe it will be found that gold production has not been sustained by this measure. Gold production has declined considerably, compared with the figures for production when the act was first passed. I do not see how the government can honestly feel that the extension of this act, now, for another four years is going to bring about a solution to this problem, any more than the legislation which has been in effect for the last 16 years has succeeded in doing so. I think we would do well to consider the state of the Canadian reserves at this time. Instead of having gold as the basis of our reserves, reliance is increasingly being placed on United States dollars with all the danger this implies to our economy. I wonder whether the government has really come to grips with this problem, or whether it has just lifted the rug and swept it underneath for another four years, feeling that the job is done.
I say that the job is not done. I think the government would be most unwise to think that this problem is solved for another four years; because it is not. As I said in this house about two weeks ago, I think it is time we adopted a new policy with regard to gold. The government should not say that
the job is done, simply because this subsidy has been extended for another four years. We should look at this problem again; we should try to come to grips with it, and make provision for a much better solution than we have reached to date.

speechtext:
The one question I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister really relates to the schedule, and since the schedule introduces a new principle into the bill I think that on second reading I can discuss it in some detail though, normally, I would not be able to do so at this stage of the bill.
In the schedule we find a list of the communities which will be able to take advantage of the act, particularly in relation to the date 1965 which, in a sense, is a cut-off date for any new mines established in areas which are not what might be called old mining communities. There is one community which is not in that list, and its absence causes me some concern. It is the community of Beardmore, Ontario, which is not far from Geraldton. There is a rich little mine there named the Leitch gold mine which is coming to the end of its productive life. Because of the quality of the ore produced at this mine it has rarely been in a position in recent years to come under the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The fact remains that this is an old gold mining community in which a considerable number of people earn their living from mining. Some of the other mines in the area, such as Northern Empire and a couple of others whose names I cannot immediately bring to memory, have been gold producers in the past and have taken advantage of this assistance. I think the minister will be able to acknowledge the truth of this from his own experience. It is not so many years ago that the Howey mine went out of production there, but the recrudescence, if I may call it that, of Red Lake causes us to realize how many lives these gold mining communities have. It looked as though Red Lake was a dead camp and unlikely to come to life again, but events proved differently. There is no question that in the general geological structure around Beardmore which runs to Geraldton, 50 miles away, a town which comes under the provisions of the act, there are prospects, which have some reality, that another producing mine may be discovered in the foreseeable future.

That is the main point I want to make.
I follow mining developments in the Northern Miner, as most people do, and there is one point which was raised in it, not too long ago, which I have brought up on previous occasions when this item was before parliament. It relates to this whole question of profits made by mines which receive assistance under this measure. I do not know what the way out of this dilemma may be. In the past it has been put to me this way by individuals-and this is the way in which it is put in the Northern Miner: certain shareholders in gold mining properties become incensed when dividends are not declared on their shares, despite the fact that companies have a profit margin as a result of gold mining subsidies. This point is made, somewhat crassly, in the Northern Miner for November 28 at page 78. A writer from the United States says:
I think that recipients of the government's costaid should distribute any profits to their shareholders and not use this money to buy one another's shares on the exchange. I feel that if a new gold subsidy is to be enacted it should state that the companies that do not pass this along to their shareholders should not be entitled to it. I own shares in both Lake Shore and Wright-Hargreaves but for many years have not received any return on this investment. Also, the price of these shares continues to sink so that I am also faced with a very heavy loss.
This is not a very important point, but it does show the dilemma of free enterprisers when any company is receiving assistance from the government. It is for this reason I should like to support the generalization of my hon. friend from Timmins (Mr. Martin) when he said the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act does not solve anything. We are presented with a continuing problem which causes trouble in the mining communities and in the capitalistic world of the mining promoters, and I would like the minister to consider putting the mines, forests and waters committee to work in an effort to come up with something better than E.G.M.A. I think our main consideration should be the communities involved.
We intend to support this measure and we have no severe criticism to make, but I do wish to remind the minister again about the Beardmore problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Hales (Wellington South) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED PAYMENT OF ASSESSMENTS BY INSTALMENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Estate Tax Act to provide for payment in appropriate cases of estate tax assessments by instalments so as to reduce the number of "forced sale" liquidations of estate assets, which in many cases have resulted in the loss of Canadian ownership and control of Canadian business enterprises.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to present this notice of motion

Estate Tax Act
at this time. It is difficult at times to get the opportunity to express one's views in the house and I appreciate having the opportunity on this occasion.
The Estate Tax Act, which came into force on January 1, 1959, was designed to replace and bring up to date the old dominion succession duty act. There is, however, one section in the new Estate Tax Act which I do not believe carries out the intention of the house. I refer to the payment of succession duties.
As hon. members know, as the act now stands these taxes must be paid in ordinary cases within six months after death. My notice of motion is in these terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Estate Tax Act to provide for payment in appropriate cases of estate tax assessments by instalments so as to reduce the number of "forced sale" liquidations of estate assets, which in many cases have resulted in the loss of Canadian ownership and control of Canadian business enterprises.
I believe a good argument could be put forward with respect to whether death duties are necessary at all. Only 1.5 per cent of the national revenue is derived from this source and in my opinion these taxes have a very crippling effect on the economy of the country. They certainly do not encourage a person to save and build up an estate. However, they are with us and probably always will be.
Therefore I think the government should give consideration to, first of all, extending the time of payment of succession duties from six months to five years and, second, making it possible to pay these taxes by instalments. As my motion deals with the payment of estate tax assessments in instalments I shall limit my remarks to this point alone.
It is of paramount importance to Canada to arrange the taxing statutes so as to encourage the retention in Canada of the ownership of Canadian enterprises and to encourage the development of capital within Canada. When the demands for taxes become confiscatory and so require the liquidation of a business at a sacrifice price, serious problems result. I submit that this is one of the reasons certain taxpayers are forsaking Canada and also why control of much of our heritage is being sold to foreign investors.
When the owner dies, in the case of a privately owned enterprise, six months is too short a time in which to secure the necessary funds to pay the succession duties. The widow or some member of the family may wish to carry on the business, but the payment of succession duties within six months is too great a drain on the capital reserve. Provided that a non-liquid estate furnishes the proper security and interest is charged on

this sum, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of permitting the payment in instalments.
May 1 remind the house again of the difficulties of continuing family or small businesses or making a satisfactory sale of the business after the death of the owner. It does create real problems. Imposing the payment of succession duties within six months, only creates further problems and causes a forced sale, the loss of ownership, often to foreign investors.
I think I should draw the attention of the house to another hardship-the payment of these taxes within six months of death causes. When the survivor, in many cases a widow, has to make a forced sale of stocks or bonds, sales have to be made at low market value and this creates serious problems for the survivor, particularly in the case of a family owned corporation.
Another hardship that is often created by imposing the present regulations under the Estate Tax Act occurs in rural areas. I know of a case where the father, the owner of a large farm stocked with purebred cattle, died without a will. Within six months, the wife passed on, leaving two sons who had worked along with their father to build up this herd of purebred cattle. Not having the ready capital to pay the succession duties, which were quite large, they were forced to hold an auction sale. This purebred herd, which took years to build, was dispersed. The results, therefore, are detrimental to the building of a sound, agricultural economy in Canada. To say the least, it is disheartening to the survivors.
In conclusion, I say what I said at the beginning, that the estate tax, in respect of the payment of succession duties, should be amended to make death taxes payable in instalments, with interest in approved cases. Several representations have been made previously to the government on this matter by the national council of women of Canada, the estate planning council of Toronto. These organizations have presented briefs to the royal commission on taxation. I hope many members of this house will endorse their views on this very important matter and the government will give serious consideration to the amendment of the Estate Tax Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Benson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUGGESTED PAYMENT OF ASSESSMENTS BY INSTALMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) in his motion implies that the necessity to pay quickly an estate tax on the value of estate property in the form of an equity in a business enterprise that contributes a significant portion of the capital of that business forces the business to raise capital by selling out, often to non-Canadians, to a degree sufficient to change the ownership and control of the business. He

also implies that if the tax due could be paid in instalments, the number of such cases would be reduced.
Although the hon. member for Wellington South is not too precise in his motion, he is presumably thinking of a business that is closely controlled, perhaps by a family group, a business that is not usually listed on the stock exchange. This government, and previous governments, have given a good deal of thought to the possible importance of the situation envisaged by the hon. member. Although individuals have from time to time asserted that there is a problem, it has been found difficult to assess its extent because there has been little or no evidence, documentary or otherwise, submitted to the government. Sometimes a family owned business is sold shortly after or shortly before the death of a principal stockholder, but it is not known whether this is because of the problem of finding enough cash to meet his estate tax liability in respect of his shares, or whether there is no one in the family who is willing or able to carry on the direction and management of the business. It is also not known to what extent such businesses are sold to non-Canadians or for what reason. What is known is that, as of last December the industrial development bank, which was given additional powers in 1961, partly with this possible situation in mind, had not made any loans or purchased shares with a view to resale or entered underwriting agreements, specifically in order to prevent the forced sale of a business because of estate taxes. Again, however, this is not completely conclusive because the industrial development bank has made loans to businesses under second and third generation ownership, to assist in the growth or consolidation of such businesses and it is not possible to be certain in how many of these cases forced sale of the business would have been thought necessary if financing had not been available from the industrial development bank. In this regard, I would refer the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), No. 648, which appeared on the order paper, and was answered earlier in the session.
Assuming that there is or was a liquidity problem, it would appear that the facilities of the industrial development bank are available in appropriate cases to solve it. In addition, there is already in the Estate Tax Act, section 16, a general provision that permits postponement of payment of tax in cases of undue hardship or excessive sacrifice. In so far as section 16 of the Estate Tax Act permits the minister to defer payment of taxes in cases of hardship which may be deemed to occur if payment is demanded too quickly, this situation may be covered. This might be useful in those rather unusual cases where
Estate Tax Act
the estates in question do not include enough of other assets, such as insurance or readily marketable securities to pay the tax, or where a loan on the assets of the business cannot be obtained. In most cases, such assets would be available in the estate of a reasonably prudent person, unless the value of the shares of the company and the tax thereon was very substantial indeed. As a matter of fact, estate planning has become more and more important during recent years, and I believe that more and more businessmen are providing for just such a situation as that envisaged by the hon. member.
There is, of course, another provision, section 15 of the Estate Tax Act, which provides for instalment payments in certain cases where the greatest liquidity problem arises. I am thinking of an estate where the sole or main asset is in the form of any income right, annuity, term of years or life or other similar estate. Generally speaking, I refer to a situation where there is a right to income in the future but no capital with which to pay the tax at present. There is not, however, any special provision for cases where there is capital but it is tied up in a family business. If a special provision were inserted in the Estate Tax Act to provide for instalment payments in such cases, this would be unfair to the estates of decedents whose property was in other forms, such as portfolio investments or real estate, or in the case of the farmer to whom the hon. member referred. Also, this would mean additional delays in the settlement of the estates affected and possible retention of the control of assets for a long time by the tax authorities.
There are also at least two other important considerations in assessing this proposal. One is that the provision of more time by allowing instalment payments of tax would likely not be of much help in meeting really large amounts of tax imposed on a large holding in a large company, for example, the holdings of Sir James Dunn in Algoma steel. The only way to be helpful in such a case, if no large liquid assets outside the business were built up over a period of time, would be to ignore the top rates of estates tax for this kind of situation. This would, of course, mean discrimination in favour of large estates and consequently could hardly be contemplated unless the rates were reduced for all estates.
The other consideration is that whatever was done in the way of relief would be offset to a considerable degree in the provinces that levy a succession duty-Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia-unless such provinces followed the federal government's lead. Another point which I think should be raised is that, beginning in 1964, the federal government has

Estate Tax Act
agreed to turn over 75 per cent of the succession duties collected to the provinces of Canada. This would mean that such a resolution, if it were considered by the government, would have to be done in consultation with the provinces, who would naturally be affected through their revenues if the payment were spread out over a longer period of time.
It should be mentioned that cognizance of this problem has been paid in the income tax law, which permits companies with large surpluses to get out the surplus by paying a modest tax, at a rate of 15 per cent, on certain conditions. In this regard I would refer the hon. member to section 105 of the Income Tax Act. The remaining tax-paid surplus can then be used to meet estate tax.
I would like to refer the hon. member to a memorandum submitted to the royal commission on banking and finance by Dr. A. K. Eaton, on October 23, 1962, and I would take the liberty of quoting from it:
It was suggested that comment might be offered in this memorandum on the problem of meeting payments called for under death duties (presumably federal estate tax and provincial inheritance taxes). The question relates not to the absolute burden of the tax but the problem of arranging affairs to have sufficient liquid assets on hand to meet the payments within the required time. Possibly the main point of concern here is whether death duties in Canada have the effect of driving the family type of business into selling out- assets or shares-to public companies, particularly foreign public companies, in order to meet tax obligations. If this were so, it would be regarded as bad.
Perhaps as a general rule it can be said that insurance is the greatest source of liquidity in estates in Canada. The addiction of Canadians to insurance is something to marvel at. It is very useful, however, as a source of ready cash to meet death duties. Normally also, most estates will show fairly substantial holdings of marketable securities, bonds which have a ready market and stocks of a type and diversity that create no problem upon fairly quick realization.
The greatest liquidity problem arises, of course, in estates where the sole or main asset is in the form of "any income right, annuity, term of years or life or other similar estate". Here, the federal law allows the tax applicable to such property to be spread over six years without interest. There are no such special provisions relating particularly to the situation where the main asset is a closely held family business-a going concern. There is, of course, a general provision in the law which gives the minister discretion to postpone tax (with interest up to 5 per cent) if he thinks the payment of it would cause "undue hardship or excessive sacrifice". It is not to be expected, however, that the necessity of selling out a family business at a fair price, where no preparation had been made by the deceased for meeting taxes on his death, would be regarded by the minister as either hardship or sacrifice. It would probably be looked upon as just plain carelessness.
In approaching this question of liquidity in the case of closely held family businesses, there is no point in attempting to sidestep the fact that death duties are very high in Canada. Plenty of family businesses are worth $1 to $2 million. The tax (federal and provincial combined) on $1 million is just over $300,000 and on $2 million, it is nearly

$800,000. From a $5 million estate, the tax would take close to half (54 per cent rate applies on excess over $2 million). Quite clearly, the so-called liquidity problem can be quite acute for estates of this size made up mainly of a single asset, a family business.
For smaller businesses, the problem is not nearly so acute. For a business worth $160,000 ($60,000 exemption for married), the tax would be $19,000. The man might have insurance enough to cover this and his son would be able to take over the business unimpaired.
An estate made up of a $260,000 business would have to pay $44,000 tax. Ordinary life insurance might not be expected to take care of all of this, so a trust company might have to be called upon to arrange for a mortgage on some of the business property for, say, $25,000. This should be practicable with no particular problem of retaining family control. Mortgage interest will, of course, cut into the flow of income to his heirs but this has to be expected. At the same time, the interest charge against the business is a deduction in computing profits for corporate tax purposes.
At the $560,000 level the problem is getting a bit worse. Here, nearly $150,000 will have to be found. Insurance can no longer be counted on to take care of much of the tax unless the deceased had been foresighted enough to have over the years taken out an insurance endowment policy specifically to meet death duties. Mortgages of higher amounts may have to be resorted to. Even so, it is reasonable to assume that up to the half million mark, there is no very good case for saying that the tax forces people to sell out a family business to a public company.
For a business of $750,000, the tax is just over $200,000, which calls for some pretty substantial financing. It would, however, still allow for a fairly reasonable equity-debt ratio for the business if a large portion of this tax liability were raised through mortgages.
Interest, of course, would be cutting deeply into earnings of the heirs but if the business were fairly profitable with good prospects, there should be no real hardship. Still, not a very good case could be made for abatement in tax provisions.
It is for estates of $1 million up that the so-called liquidity problem becomes acute. It was mentioned above that for a $1 million estate, the tax is over $300,000, for $2 million, nearly $800,000 and for $5 million, about $2.5 million. One cannot expect that tax money in these proportions will be available without careful planning a long time ahead. For the $5 million estate, it is too much to expect to have business as usual after the government has taken away half of it. Such a family business could only be continued as such if over a period of a good many years the proprietor had systematically built up a heavy position of liquid assets outside the business. He may have decided long ago that it was not worth it and accordingly, today finds himself among those who complain about taxation closing up his family business, having to sell out to pay tax. It is, of course, next to impossible to get a decent price for unlisted minority shares in a family controlled business.
Dr. Eaton continues on, and in the final paragraph of his submission he says:
Today the corporate tax on income up to $35,000 is only 21 per cent, with a 20 per cent dividend tax credit. This is fairly lenient tax treatment. The proprietor of the business can then gradually create tax paid undistributed income on hand and thus put himself in a position to borrow money on mortgage from his business and provide liquid funds for meeting estate tax. It is suggested here

that the way has been paved as far as is reasonably possible to enable family control of businesses in Canada to be maintained.
This was a submission by Dr. A. K. Eaton who used to be deputy minister of finance. To sum up, it would seem to be very difficult to ascertain or define the "appropriate cases" to which the hon. member refers in his motion, without discrimination; that the industrial development bank has been placed in a position to give the assistance envisaged by the motion in deserving cases; and that it is doubtful if anything more can be done without extensive revision of the provisions of the Estate Tax Act dealing with the time for payment and the rate structure, and without provincial co-operation.
