speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion moved by the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales). Little did I think when I used to pal around with his uncle at college in 1909 that I would be supporting a motion of his in the House of Commons in 1963. Before proceeding I must congratulate the parliamentary secretary on his magnificent and curate-like reading of the liturgy prepared by the income tax department for this motion. I thought he did it very well. In fact he reminded me of a curate preaching a sermon to a questionable couple he has just married, and he is not quite certain about the future life they will lead.
First, let me say that the hon. member has introduced this motion as a result of discussions with his constituents and a knowledge of the hardship that has been experienced. I do not quite understand the resistance offered to the motion by the parliamentary secretary, in view of its very reasonable terms. I shall not read all the motion but it asks for consideration to be given "to amending the Estate Tax Act to provide for payment in appropriate cases of estate tax assessments by instalments so as to reduce the number of 'forced sale' liquidations of estate assets ..."
It is asking consideration for a problem many people face. I listened carefully to what the parliamentary secretary read. He used several arguments and mentioned the industrial development bank as a source to borrow money. Let me remind him the time limit is six months, and it usually takes from a year to two years to negotiate a loan from the industrial development bank. I know that, because several constituents of mine have mentioned their problems to me.
Then he said there was a provision which provides for postponement of the payment of these death duties in cases of hardship. Mr. Speaker, just try it, and see how long it takes you to get the question of hardship recognized
Estate Tax Act
by the department. I must say that the parliamentary secretary speaks from the viewpoint of the Department of Finance. From listening to his remarks, on that point, and the others which he read, I take it there is a complete lack of understanding that this is a problem faced by a good many people in small businesses and on family farms.
The parliamentary secretary read at great length from a submission prepared by Dr. Eaton, and suggested one should arrange one's affairs in such a way as to have liquid assets to meet these taxes. Does not the hon. gentleman know that you can be farming on quite a small scale, and successfully in that you are paying your way, and you can be running a small family business successfully but very often such operations, carried on in some cases from generation to generation because they provide a living for the families concerned, have made very little profit at the end of the year? These are the persons who are affected. Dr. Eaton suggests, through using the hon. gentleman as his mouthpiece this evening, that in such cases insurance should be taken out by the families concerned. But very often there is not sufficient profit to provide the insurance required to meet these death duties, which can be quite substantial and have increased rapidly in recent years. There are many properties that were considered in the first instance to cost very little but which have developed throughout the years, and because of inflated values now have a very much higher value than was the case ten years ago.
This presents a problem to the small business people or the family farm. I know what I am talking about because I have spoken to constituents who fear this sort of thing. I am quite sure that the hon. gentleman who introduced this motion is also aware of this problem, and has met persons who have suffered because of the present Estate Tax Act. We are not talking about the wealthy people with whom the hon. gentleman was more concerned, because he mentioned persons who had $500,000 or $1 million. We are concerned with the little people. This particular problem does not arise with large organizations; they have liquid assets such as bonds and shares that can be sold. It is when one has to sell a family concern or farm that real hardship is created. These small businesses and farms have to be sold to meet the present taxes.
In supporting this motion, Mr. Speaker, I claim that the present law does not give consideration to the immediate responsibilities of the heirs and the problems they face, particularly in the smaller income groups that have been mentioned. Second, the present

Estate Tax Act
legislation gives no consideration to the economic value to the country and the community of these small businesses and family farms, and in some cases small industry. I know small saw mill operators who have carried on quite successfully, not making much money, employing men from year to year and investing capital now and again in order to continue their operation. These people do not make much profit. They are people whose God is not the almighty dollar. They like to accept their responsibilities to the community. There is no consideration given to the economic value of these small businesses, family farms and so on. With those few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I conclude what I have to say, because I know there are other hon. members who wish to express their support for this very reasonable and practical motion.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PAYMENT OF ASSESSMENTS BY INSTALMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house is considering now a motion which we are very happy to support, and I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) for having introduced it.
The motion urges the government to amend the Estate Tax Act in order to prevent the forced sale liquidation of many family business enterprises. In fact, Mr. Speaker, how many family businesses or industries, for instance, have been liquidated in Canada, especially in French Canada, owing to the implementation of the unfair Estate Tax Act? It would be really interesting to gather such information, because I know that we have suffered greatly from that situation, we of the province of Quebec, owing to the family type of business so popular in that province.
Mr. Speaker, family businesses have always been popular in the province of Quebec because they are consistent with French humanism. That is why most businesses or industries in Quebec are owned by families.
To date, we have many times witnessed the liquidation of businesses because the heirs or the executors had to sell some properties in order to pay estate duties. If legislation to provide for instalment payments of succession duties were enacted, it could help to correct a situation which has been truly disastrous, I would say in Canada, especially in French Canada.
And at this stage of my remarks, may I recall a great historic event to the attention of the house? It is that in 1760, just prior to the transfer of Canada to England, French Canadians had almost 100 million pounds of fiduciary money in circulation. Now, after the transfer of Canada, they were almost entirely
[Mr. Herridge.)
dispossessed owing to the new currency introduced in the country by the invaders. And it is only through the amount of work done by French-Canadian families that family, commercial and industrial wealth was restored and that there was gradually developed a type of family business which, as I just said, was consistent with French humanism, with the French type of business.
Today, many businesses are turning to the Anglo-Saxon or capitalistic type of company because there is a propaganda urging French Canadian industrialists and businessmen to operate as public companies, especially to protect themselves against the problem of succession duties.
In my opinion, it is very unfortunate that
we have to change this type of business which was the backbone of our people. However, for our own protection, we have to move toward this type of public companies, otherwise we would go on losing what we have succeeded in gaining, as we lost perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars in the past.
I hope that the commission which is inquiring into fiscal matters-I believe it is the Carter commission-will come up with practical solutions to reduce succession duties, for it is illogical that so many people and families who have acquired some property should be dispossessed in such a drastic fashion.
I feel that family property is sacred and I submit that governments have no right to dispossess families that way. That is why the Social Credit party is happy to support this motion which would slightly improve the present taxation system. We must go further than that, however; we must enact new legislation to bring about a considerable reduction in succession duties and taxes.
If all hon. members would take the trouble to examine the development of the monetary system throughout the ages, they might come to understand a little more easily how we passed, for instance, from the premonetary period to the bimetallism period, then to the fiduciary currency period and on to the credit money we have now in 1963-and God knows that credit money is practically the only one in circulation nowadays. Then we could proceed with monetary reforms allowing us to reduce the burden of enterprises, individuals and families.

Mr. Speaker, I will only take a few moments to bring forward some of the reasons for my great interest in this motion. As a matter of fact, it was with a certain feeling of nostalgia that I listened to our genial hon. friend, the

parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) give reasons that I have heard many times in this regard. I will not be at all reticent, Mr. Speaker, in telling the house that over the years I have advocated the principle of this particular motion. However, as with many other things, one sometimes has to wait a little longer for the better things in life.
I was interested, first of all, in the alternatives that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance indicated were available to businessmen under the Industrial Development Bank Act. I fully appreciate the attempt which was made in amending the Industrial Development Bank Act, but let me say this: it does not go far enough. I was fully aware that there have been no applications for this type of loan under the act. I know that in one case where application was made to protect a financial business worth at that time an estimated $3 million it was subsequently sold for $20 million. True, we are dealing with a big asset, but it is one where there had to be a sale and it was sold to foreign investment merely by reason of fear of the estate tax and the impossibility at that time of making adequate provision.
Dr. Eaton has a very theoretical and nice sounding proposition in the lengthy quotations we got from the parliamentary secretary, but this presupposes that owners of a concern are master of all the factors and that they can plan to the nth degree. Let me assure him that I am concerned with companies where one cannot do so. I can cite the case of one of our better growth companies, controlled by four men in their forties, which had to be sold to what I am sure was foreign capital because the principal shareholder could not get any insurance. He was uninsurable. This was a growth company where there were no accumulated reserves. The principals drew good salaries but their capital was tied up in the shares of that company and its subsidiaries. If you cannot get a term insurance with a buy-sell agreement, how can you protect the interests of the estate and the remaining shareholders who must make some provision for eventualities? There was no doubt in my mind that against the potential assets of the principal shareholders of this company there was going to be a substantial tax assessment. I know of other cases where Canadians have lost control. I am not going to name the companies; they come through knowledge acquired in my legal practice.
I would draw to the attention of the parliamentary secretary the discussion which took place in the taxation section of the Canadian bar convention this year. There were any
Estate Tax Act
number of representations in this regard. I find that most of the arguments against the principle are of an administrative nature. I would say that, in the case of a company, where there is an opportunity of getting an extension under section 16, there may not be too much sympathy shown on the part of the Minister of National Revenue. This is being realistic. It is my view that we should be able to make the appropriate changes in the act to provide for these cases, not only those referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), but the much larger growth businesses of this country. I know at least half a dozen good companies which had to be sold. There was such an attractive offer of outside capital and, by that, I mean foreign capital, that on balance they said: Why put up with the worry about estate tax? Let us get the money now and we shall be able to sleep a lot more easily.
The parliamentary secretary spoke about the difficulties of retention of control. I think in the case of most of these companies the surviving owners are prepared to pay at least a proportion of the estate tax that is due. The balance can be put even on a basis of ten years, on annual instalments with interest. There is no doubt in my mind that with the continuing shareholders or the remaining shareholders carrying on the business, the business will stand a better chance of success than if it were to pass into other hands.
Now I come to this matter of payment to the provinces and the suggestion that the provinces would have to be consulted. But have they acquired a vested interest? I would say it goes only to the question of moneys paid in to the crown under the heading of estate tax or succession duties, and that a vested interest is not acquired in any estate whether within the boundaries of a particular province or otherwise. I am sure the act does not provide for that, nor do any of the agreements and, therefore, I cannot see that this question of the consent of the provinces would have anything to do with the matter. The provinces will ultimately get the money. This was an argument which did not carry much weight as far as I am concerned.
I think we have canvassed this problem sufficiently. I do feel that sufficient reason has been shown that the appropriate amendments should have been made to the act or at least been more seriously considered in the past. I am sorry the parliamentary secretary came to us with a speech or memorandum prepared on the basis of a closed mind in this regard rather than with a conciliatory, "we will have a good look at it". I think we should take a much better look at this question than we

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act have in the past, and I would ask members of the house to consider the resolution on that basis.

speechtext:
When I first read the motion of the hon. member for Wellington South to amend the Estate Tax Act, the words "forced sale" intrigued me. As to the allegation that the severity of this act resulted, in many cases, in the loss of control of Canadian companies to foreigners, my first reaction was that this was not so. After looking into the matter I remain unconvinced. There have been some cases where the necessity of paying estate tax and provincial succession duty has been cited as the reason, or an additional reason, for selling a controlling interest in a company to foreigners or to a foreign company. This seems strange when one knows that any company with good management can easily make arrangements to pay the taxes due to both jurisdictions.
When one hears such talk he should consider whether or not an excuse is being given by an incapable or disinterested heir for his failure to assume an unexpected or unwanted responsibility. I would say from my own experience that in almost every case of such a sale the real reason is that death has brought about an unusual circumstance. There has been a change of management or there has been no management left whatever.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Benson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING LOAN PERIOD, ESTABLISHING NEW PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill contains amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act which would enable the banks to continue making business improvement loans under this act beyond the end of the year. The present authority in the act for government guarantees of such loans expires on December 31, 1963. Legislative action must be taken now if guaranteed lending operations are to continue beyond that date.
Hon. members will recall that the royal commission on banking and finance was established in 1961 to undertake a broad review of the functioning of the Canadian financial system. The commission is expected to report within the next few months, and it can be anticipated that the commission has reviewed the whole question of financial facilities available to business, including small business enterprises. We have decided, in the circumstances, not to undertake an over-all review of this act until we can do so in the light of the report and recommendations of this commission. The proposed bill before us is accordingly limited to extending the act for another three years and to some clarifying amendments to the security provisions of this act, which can be usefully made at this time.
The Small Businesses Loans Act was passed three years ago to provide term credit for a wide range of business improvement projects to the proprietors of small business enterprises engaged in manufacturing, wholesale

Small Businesses Loans Act and retail trade, and in service industries. Loans of this type are made by the chartered banks with a government guarantee. The act limits the guarantee in effect during the current lending period, that is since inception to December 31, 1963, to a maximum of 10 per cent of the total of all secured loans made under the act by each bank, provided the aggregate principal amount of all guaranteed loans made by all banks does not exceed $300 million. In effect, this limits the government's maximum contingent liability in respect of losses on business improvement loans to $30 million.
During the first year of operations, in 1961, some 2,800 guaranteed loans totalling $25.6 million were made by the banks to small business enterprises. The number and volume of loans made under the act during 1962 were of similar magnitude, close to 3,000 loans totalling $25.7 million. Complete figures for 1963 are, of course, not yet available.
Turning to the specific provisions of the bill, clause 1 would amend subsection 2 of section 3 of the act to change the date to which guaranteed loans can be made from December 31, 1963, to December 31, 1966.
The Small Businesses Loans Act, like the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, on which it was modelled, runs in three-year periods.
Clause 2 would amend sections 5 and 6 of the act to provide an additional lending period, extending from January 1, 1964 to December 31, 1966, during which guaranteed business improvement loans may be made by the chartered banks on the same terms and conditions as those applying to loans made during the first lending period. It also specifies that the aggregate sum of total business improvement loans which may be made during this period by all banks under the government guarantee is $300 million, the same limit which applied to the first lending period.
Clause 3 of the bill deals with section 8, the security provision of the act. This section, in general, empowers the bank to take mortgage security, including chattel mortgage, on loans made under this act notwithstanding section 88 of the Bank Act. Some questions on the legal interpretation of this section have, however, arisen in the course of lending experience, and it is considered desirable, following consultation with the bankers association, to clarify section 8 in two respects. First, the proposed new section 8 would make it explicit that the Quebec commercial pledge comes within the scope of this section. The commercial pledge is a civil code concept comparable to chattel mortgage, which was made applicable to business by Quebec legislation earlier this year. The second change

in section 8 would make it clear that mortgage securities can be taken not only as direct security for the repayment of a loan, but also in support of an endorsement or a guarantee given by a third party.
I am sure that hon. members will agree that the guarantee provisions of the act should be extended and that a review of its adequacy and effectiveness should be deferred pending the report of the royal commission on banking and finance. I can assure the house that it would be the government's intention to review the provisions of this act in some detail and to propose whatever changes are considered desirable after it has had an opportunity to consider the report of the commission, and that such a review will take into account comments and suggestions which have been or may be made in the house, as well as those of the business and banking community.

speechtext:
I am sure the house appreciates the statement made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in respect of this bill. This measure, primarily, extends the period of an act which was introduced by the government of three years ago and carries it on for another three years. I am sure the house appreciates the figures which have just been given to us by the parliamentary secretary indicating the number of loans which have been made under this act.
I have a fairly clear recollection of statements which were made when the original bill was introduced. Hon. members said that this bill would be of little effect and that no advantage would be taken of it by the people of Canada. The figures which have been read tonight by the parliamentary secretary show how wrong those statements were, as have most of the statements which have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite. Even the statement made by hon. members opposite when they were in the opposition were to the effect that this act should not be enacted. This was just another one of the steps taken by the preceding government which resulted in expanding the economy of this country, the benefit of which this government is receiving at this moment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we shall support these amendments, which are very necessary but rather minor. I am pleased to hear the parliamentary secretary state that a more thorough revision of this act is now under way, because it certainly needs it. Some points which I think might well be considered are, a better rate of interest for small businesses receiving loans under the act; the amounts might well be increased; and there is another aspect, that is

that the loans cannot be received for establishing a new business. They are only for existing businesses. There are a number of cases in which people have bought into old businesses, and not very good ones, in order to qualify for a loan under the act. There are a number of things of this nature which I think might well be reviewed.
I was checking the debates on this topic, Mr. Speaker, when the act was amended back in 1961. I noticed two very important Liberals were interested at that time, namely the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). They made a number of suggestions to the effect that you could improve or strengthen the act. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would refer those to the minister when this matter comes up for review. They described the act as inadequate and puny in some respects.
I should like also, Mr. Speaker, to mention to the parliamentary secretary that it is one thing to give help to small businesses in the way of loans so that they can become established, but it is another thing to keep them going. I hope that somewhere along the line the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will consult with his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier), with a view to strengthening our anti-combines legislation. I shall not go very far into this tonight, but I want to speak about it again when the justice estimates are under discussion.
It seems to me rather useless to give this aid to small business on the one hand and then leave them prey to very weak combines legislation such as we have now. I should like to suggest, too, that when this department makes a report on the Small Businesses Loans Act they try to make the report a little more complete. I have in front of me the annual report for 1962, which is a very poor document. There is a small amount of statistical material, but that is all. There is not really very much meat here. I think it would be very useful if we could get some examples of the type of business which has been assisted by this measure. This report is very meagre and inadequate.
However, to conclude, I may say I had a speech prepared on the basis of the fact that the legislation needs looking at, but I shall forgo making that speech tonight since we have the assurance that the act will be reviewed after the royal commission on taxation reports. Meantime, we support the proposed amendments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party intend to support the amendments that have been proposed by the parliamentary secretary. He said that the
28902-5-358
Small Businesses Loans Act act originally was to be of the same value to small businesses as the farm improvement loans legislation and other acts are to farmers and fishermen. However my experience with the Small Businesses Loans Act indicates it is not administered in the same way as the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
For example, we note there are some minor amendments broadening the basis for security, in the changes that are suggested. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act a bank takes security only on the piece of equipment that is being purchased. In some cases it is necessary for a farmer to pay down 25 per cent or 30 per cent of the price, while the balance is financed over a period of from three to five years. Even if the farmer's credit rating is blemished a little, he is still able to avail himself of the provisions of the act, and small businesses should receive the same treatment.
I find that in many cases when a small business operator goes to a bank he finds there is no additional consideration given him, even though this act is in force. In other words, if a man's credit rating is not good enough for him to qualify under regular bank requirements for security, he is unable to get a loan under this act. Therefore I am pleased that the parliamentary secretary says the act is going to be reviewed and the basis for security should be broadened and extended. I did not hear him say the review would take place next session, in 1964, but I certainly hope that is the intention of the government. We give credit to whomever it was initiated this act, but I do not believe the practical application of it has been as extensive as was intended.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING LOAN PERIOD, ESTABLISHING NEW PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we greatly appreciate the amendments contained in Bill No. C-122 which tends to be more beneficial to small businesses in Canada.
In the past three years, many small businesses have been assisted through this legislation which, as the former minister of finance pointed out a while ago, was passed by the Conservative government and is now being renovated by a Liberal administration.
We are not interested in knowing which party did what, but we are greatly interested in the matter of loans granted to small businesses. While many small businesses received assistance, several others did not get any. They were asked to fill out forms, to offer guarantees and then their cases were subjected to unending studies.
The point I want to make is this. We have, for instance, the industrial development bank which assists small businesses and

Small Businesses Loans Act even large ones and which lends money at higher rates than those of the chartered banks but for a longer period.
This bill will allow the chartered banks to ask for more collateral from people and small industries which apply for loans, for expansion purposes or to keep their business going.
How is it that the Bank of Canada, or the industrial development bank asks for a higher interest rate than the chartered banks and how is it that the same industrial development bank does not assume greater risks as far as small industries are concerned?
There are small businessmen, small shopkeepers who are confronted with hardship, who are faced with a dreadful situation, in our country, in every province.
Why does Bill No. C-122 not stipulate that both the Bank of Canada and the industrial development bank are authorized to assume more risks in order to give more help to small businesses, even if hundreds of them have already been helped in the past?
We will certainly support the proposed amendments, but we would like to see the government take action to facilitate access to more credit for small businesses, because the help granted is often inadequate. Then a small industry or a small businessman cannot go very far. The point is to lend them more and at a reasonable rate of interest, that is a rate of interest that will not dispossess them.
Mr. Speaker, we support the proposed amendments, but at the same time we suggest that the government should as much as possible place the industrial development bank at the disposal of these industries and small businessmen, with an adequate and reasonable rate of interest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill gives me an opportunity to say a few words about the success of the operations under the Small Businesses Loans Act which was introduced in 1960 and became really effective in 1961. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) was not sure who introduced it. I would like to tell him it was the former minister of finance, the Hon. Donald Fleming, in 1960, the same year that so much good legislation was put on the statute books.
My hon. friend from Wellington (Mr. Hales) who sits behind me, and who saw I was about to speak, warned me not to forget to tell how important the act has been for the tourist industry. I recall the many times I, and others, had the privilege of advocating assistance for service establishments to improve their accommodation and services to the travelling public. With the introduction of this legislation, and the inclusion of service establishments under it, tourist operations received a substantial lift.
The annual report for 1962 on the Small Businesses Loans Act, which came into our hands within the last few days, shows on page 10, under the heading "Loans to service businesses", that a total of 1,246 loans were made in the amount of $12,313,000. This means that 1,246 tourist operators, restaurant owners, motel and lodge operators have made substantial improvements to their establishments under the provisions of this act, and this accounts in no small part for the wonderful improvement we see in accommodation as we travel throughout the country. Just about the time this act was passed, the travel bureau was making a tremendous effort to reverse our deficit in travel account with the United States. In the year following the enactment of that legislation-although I know it was not entirely responsible-and in this current year there has been a wonderful improvement in our balance of payments in travel account. I will not go into that aspect now, except to state that it has improved. I think the fact that visitors have better accommodation, better restaurants and better facilities throughout encourages them to come to Canada and take advantage of the services that we have to offer.
It is not only the service businesses which have benefited, but also small businesses generally. On the same page of the annual report it is indicated that a total of 923 loans were made to the retail trade, totalling $7,710,000. The significant part of this report in tables 5 and 6 is that while the act was originally intended for the retail trade and small business, several of us who were

particularly interested in the tourist business prevailed upon the government, and in particular the minister of finance, to include service businesses in the act. This was done, and the minister at that time honoured me by acknowledging the efforts I had made. The significant part is that there were actually more loans made to service businesses than to the retail trades, which I think proves the advantage of including the service businesses in this act.
That is all I want to say on the bill, Mr. Speaker. We certainly approve the principle of extending the provisions of the act for a further period of time. There are still shortcomings in the legislation and they have become apparent as the act has been administered. I am glad to hear there is to be a review once again of the Small Businesses Loans Act and I hope we may be able to put it in a little better shape after the experiment of just over two years. The figures I have given of the total amount of loans actually only cover a period of one year, and I think this is indicative of the benefits Canadians have reaped from the Small Businesses Loans Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my feelings about this amendment to the small business loans legislation.
I am pleased to see that the act is under review. That is why I want to participate in this debate and I should ask the Minister of Finance or his representative to consider how the amended legislation will be applied.
It is probably because this act was encumbered with red tape that it did not help small businesses as much as it should have.
It was a complicated act for those who wanted to secure a loan: they had to submit applications, fill out forms and submit to extensive investigations. I believe that such red tape has prevented many businesses to take advantage of that assistance.
I would like this bill to be considered in the light of the planning which has been proposed by the present government.
I wonder what those celebrated planning experts within the government are waiting for? They have stood in the forefront to sell the idea of planning as being a panacea. I see some of those experts: I see one in particular who has been formerly with the department of industry of the province of Quebec. I wonder what they are doing at the present time in the planning of industry in Canada so as to check unemployment as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I think this Small Businesses Loans Act is a formula through which the
28902-5-358J
Small Businesses Loans Act present government can not only help already established businesses but mainly help towards the establishment of new ones. I think they could give special encouragement if they could provide a special interest rate in the case of businesses which would be engaged in the production of consumers' goods or of some small industrial machinery.
I think the industries setting up in the services sector are also useful. But I think at this time, we mostly need small businesses involved in the production of smallwares which are consumed every day in the country and which can be bought only on foreign markets. All we see is "made in Japan", "made in Italy", "made in France" or "made in England". We seldom see "made in Canada" as far as smallwares are concerned.
That, I believe, is the field of small businesses. In the old countries, the small enterprise is a major factor of stabilization thanks to which unemployment is inexistent, because they develop readily when they have some incentives.
Such encouragement, Mr. Speaker, is up to the hon. members opposite and to the planning officers to give. I think that it is in the matter of interests, that adequate incentive can be given to those small undertakings. They can also be given incentive in terms of taxation. I believe that the income tax reports they have to file to meet the requirements of the government should be simplified.
Mr. Speaker, my suggestion should be taken into consideration by everyone, if we wish that this legislation providing assistance to small businesses meet the purposes for which it is intended, namely to help existing businesses. Furthermore, it is our duty to stimulate our industrialists and to encourage them to invest and establish the industries required at the present time in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make what might be termed a miniature speech. I rise to support the principle and purpose of this bill, which includes some necessary amendments as a first step to further amendments that we look forward to in the very near future. I want to say a few words on this matter because I see the parliamentary secretary is, shall I say, closer to the opposition in respect of the terms of this legislation than he was in the debate that occurred between five and six o'clock and I am going to take the opportunity to make a few suggestions in view of the review promised by the parliamentary secretary on behalf of the government.
This type of legislation was advocated for years by members of this party and we were glad when the former government originally

Small Businesses Loans Act introduced this act and also legislation to improve credit facilities for farmers. We must give them credit for that; they were both steps in the right direction. We look upon this as pilot legislation. This is the foundation upon which can be built an act that really works and serves the purposes for which it was enacted. It requires considerable amendment to meet various types of small business and small industry local conditions and circumstances. I have had some experience of the matter through discussing this act with retailers and small business people who have taken advantage of it, and a great many more who were unable to take advantage of it because of its present terms.
In view of the review that has been promised by the parliamentary secretary I am just going to take a few minutes to lay the groundwork for the philosophy which I think should govern the review when it is undertaken by the government. The development of monopoly control in business, with its consequent effect on small business, has been recognized in Canada for years. As I mentioned before, members of this party sought legislation of this kind for over 25 years in this house. I have read some of the speeches made in the house by the first members of this party. The retail merchants of Canada and other organizations made representations to government after government before they were able to get the legislation accepted by the government, or at least the pilot legislation put on the statute books of Canada. Then the government, commencing in 1956, published a small business manual, which I think was again published in 1957 and 1959. Later the small business branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce was established. The legislation that we are considering this evening followed those steps. I hope the parliamentary secretary is listening, because I want to quote some very good authorities. It may interest him to know that even John Buchan, former governor general of Canada, recognized this problem in his book "Pilgrim's Way" in 1940, in which he has this to say about the basic dilemma that confronts us now:
Somehow or other, we must make our social and economic world more fluid. We must widen the approaches so that honest ambition and honourable discontent may have elbow room. The world must remain an oyster for youth to open. If not, youth will cease to be young, and that will be the end of everything.
I think that is very well put. The problems in small business have been considered in the United States and in other countries for some years. We are not alone in facing this problem. It is one which has developed because of the needs of a changing society. A cabinet committee in the United States made


a report on small business in 1956. I think this is what prompted us to take action. In addition, a good deal of literature has been published on this subject. I wish to conclude by quoting from the United States report I do not often go to the United States for my quotations but I think this one is particularly apt:
Now is the time for all good men, regardless of party, to come to the aid of small business. The good society of the future which we seek in the face of war's terrible sacrifices cannot exist without small business, and small business cannot fulfill its part unless the necessary steps are taken to allow it the opportunity to function. This means giving it access to capital, especially equity capital, the vigorous enforcement of anti-monopoly laws, and encouragement in the way of tax relief or incentives.	.
Once again we must choose. Either we wish to maintain free enterprise, modified in the course of industrial evolution to fit a twentieth century abruptly with our traditions to embrace a society of big business only, with cartelization and monopoly as accepted features.
I think that is very well put when one considers the source of the quotation. Members of this group believe that socially desirable free enterprise, where the genuine element of competition has free play, has a significant and important role to perform within the framework of a democratic and socialist planned economy directed towards definite economic and social objectives and designed to provide peace, plenty and progress for all.
In concluding I suggest that the review which it is proposed to undertake should include an extensive study of the operations of this act across Canada in various regions and in various fields. I have found that in many cases small business people require more information. I was talking to a businessman in Trail this summer. He had spent $25,000 improving his premises and then he applied for a loan under this legislation in order to buy stock. If he had been informed as to the situation he would have borrowed the money to improve his premises and kept his capital to buy his stock. That was unfortunate. I am familiar with other instances of local businessmen, sound men in their own enterprises, who lack an understanding of the operation of this act. I draw this situation to the attention of the parliamentary secretary. Again, I find that some bank managers are not too co-operative. I know four or five cases where businessmen who went to a bank intending to take advantage of the provisions of the act were, to some extent, cold shouldered. As a result, they applied to the credit union in that city to borrow the money that was necessary, in some cases up to $10,000, and without difficulty, because their enterprises were sound. On the other hand, some managers were co-operative and

anxious to inform local businessmen as to the terms of the act and how they could take advantage of it.
I suggest that some of the officials of the department should visit certain regions and become acquainted with the opportunities which exist there for the expansion of small business. In the constituency from which I come there is an opportunity for the expansion of small lumber businesses. Other men are in the logging industry contracting for larger companies. There are opportunities for the expansion of the tourist industry. I know a few tourist operators who have been taking advantage of this act; the loans have been of benefit to them. I know others who could not qualify because of particular circumstances.
In conclusion I would urge, again, that the department send some of these officials out into the field. There is nothing like talking to these people. It would be a good idea to get in touch with businessmen's organizations, chambers of commerce and farmers' organizations interested in business in a small way, in a co-operative way. Thus the officials would get a picture of the numbers and the kind of people whom this measure is intended to serve. It might also be a good idea to have a school for bankers, perhaps one school in each province. The purpose of the act could be explained at these schools, and the suggestions of those attending could be sought. I am sure that in this way we could greatly improve this pilot legislation so that, ultimately, it would perform the function it is intended to perform.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING LOAN PERIOD, ESTABLISHING NEW PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext: The definition is as follows: a mortgage is the creature of English common law, as used in the other nine provinces; hypothec is a creature of the civil code as used exclusively in Quebec. In a mortgage the title in the property passes from the man who owns the land to the mortgagee, the man lending the money. Under the hypothec the ownership does not pass. From a lawyer's standpoint there are two entirely different concepts arising from two entirely different codes of law, and when the hon. member for Lapointe says mortgage is unknown in the civil code he is perfectly correct. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with respect to this bill. As I have indicated, my interest is solely in a point of order and not in the substance of the bill itself. One of the best known rules of this House of Commons is that a money bill must be preceded by a resolution. All of us who are private members of course know this, for it certainly applies to any bills that we seek to bring in. It also applies to bills brought in by the government. This, I may say, arises not just from a standing order of the House of Commons or from some citation in Beauchesne, but rather from section 54 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
That principle is carried forward in standing order 61 of the standing orders of the House of Commons, which says the same thing in standing order language, so that I need not repeat it. This principle is also confirmed in two or three citations in Beauchesne's-rather, I should say it is confirmed in a dozen citations, but I call attention to only two or three of them. I am looking at Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 243, which says:
All bills providing for the payment of salaries or for any expenditure whatever out of the public funds of the dominion must be first considered as resolutions in committee of the whole.
Similarly citation 355 of Beauchesne's fourth edition says:
Bills involving expenditure of public money or taxation, and all measures involving a charge upon the people must be preceded by a resolution.
As hon. members are aware, Bill No. C-120 is one of a number of bills that first reached us on Friday. We did not know at that time what the bill would contain. I recognize that the point upon which I base my point of order might seem to be a small one, but the principle is one that I think we must recognize. The bill includes provision for increasing the number of directors of the body established by it. Though they do not receive any remuneration, they receive their expenses;

World Exhibition Corporation Act but in addition to that I would point out that for the commissioner general and the deputy commissioner general there has been added money for allowances. By the previous act they were provided with salaries but not allowances, but provision is now made for the commissioner general and the deputy commissioner general to receive allowances as fixed by the governor in council. I have read through the bill itself-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could ask the hon. member a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: Surely.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman considered who is to pay these salaries?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: I cannot say that I have read in detail on that particular point, but it has been provided in this legislation, and the act we are now amending was brought before parliament as a money bill with a preceding resolution.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: That was a grant to a corporation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: But the provision for these salaries and allowances is to be made by the governor in council. It is really improper for me to go into the sections of the bill at this point, except to make the reference to the fact that it is the governor in council that fixes the amount of the salaries and allowances these people are to receive. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if this is the case this bill, even though it is a minor point financially, should have been preceded by a resolution.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in commenting on the different points raised by the hon. member. I think he has established very clearly that a money bill should be preceded by a resolution. There is no ambiguity there. But may I point out to the hon. member that on December 20, 1962, the act was passed and in section 11 it is provided that a grant not exceeding $20 million will be paid from time to time to the corporation of the world fair. Bill No. C-120 which is now before us makes a few minor amendments to the act. May I point out to the hon. member that any remuneration not provided for in the previous act will be paid out of the fund voted under that act. We are not looking for any additional funds; the funds have been voted and we are now asking for a few amendments to be made. I do not think that under these circumstances the jurisprudence quoted by the hon. member applies to this bill.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that members of the privy council both


present and former will realize that even if additional money is not asked for, the government can only spend money or assign money to those purposes for which parliament has given approval. This applies to estimates; the fact that a total sum of money has been voted does not give the government power to move that money from one item to another.
I submit that the act passed last December stated certain purposes for which this $20 million could be used. One of those purposes was the salaries of these two people. There was no suggestion in that act that any of this money could be used for the purpose which is now spelled out in the bill before us. I submit that even though not another dollar may be necessary to carry out these purposes, what we now have is a bill indicating a purpose which was not envisioned in the previous legislation. That is the nub of section 54 of the British North America Act, that there cannot be such a vote of money for any purposes that has not been first recommended to the house by message of the governor in council. I recognize that there may be no additional money involved. If there is additional money involved, it will have to be brought in in some other way later on. But a new purpose has been imported into the legislation that was not in the legislation when it was introduced last year.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out to the hon. member that in the act passed on November 20, 1962 there was provision for the remuneration of officers of the world fair corporation; but no amount was mentioned, this being left to the discretion of the governor in council. I think-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: But there was no provision for allowances; that is something new that is being asked for. If it is not something new, why is it being asked for?

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: I only want to add a word to this, Mr. Speaker. I think that once the funds are voted by parliament we should not require a resolution if we wish to bring in amendments to an act. I believe the points of order raised by my hon. friend have no application in this situation.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it may be useful if I refer to a reference in Beau-chesne's third edition at page 479 which certainly supports the point of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and says:
Another element which places this measure in the category of money bills is that its adoption would mean the transfer of the authority under which appropriated money is to be spent.

Further it says:
When money is voted, the main conditions imposed on its expenditure are embodied in resolutions. All the circumstances concerning its destination lorm part ot the appropriation with which they are considered and if any alteration is to be made it must be by the same process as the original resolution.
Then it says that the circumstances under which an expenditure is to be made are indivisible from that expenditure.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if at the time you are considering this question you would take this point into account. I raise it specifically because of the contention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) to the effect that once an allocation of money is made and set out in the statute, you do not need any further resolution amending or changing the manner in which that money will be spent. I do not have the specific reference, but during the session of 1962-63 when Mr. Speaker Lambert was in the chair I had introduced a bill seeking to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act to say that moneys expended under that act could be used for the purposes of highways other than the specifically designated trans-Canada highway. The amount of money was provided by a previous amendment to the statute. I in no way sought to have the amending bill changed, or alter that amount of money; merely that it could be expended with the approval of the governor in council for another purpose, another type of highway, in the same way as this bill now before us seeks to say that the amount of money provided by a previous statute can be expended in another way, namely for allowances.
Mr. Speaker Lambert ruled the bill I had introduced to be out of order on precisely the same grounds as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is saying that this bill is out of order. I appealed Mr. Speaker Lambert's decision. We had a division. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) was then a private member and he and every one of his Liberal colleagues then in the house voted to support the ruling of Mr. Speaker Lambert, though they are now singing a different tune.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I may say a word on this. It does not seem to me that the hon. member has drawn a true analogy, because what he was seeking to do on that occasion- and I remember it very well-was to change the purpose for which money could be expended out of the treasury. In this case parliament made a grant of $20 million to a corporation. The grant has been made. There is no suggestion that anything be added to it and there is mo suggestion that the money be used for any other purpose apart from the
World Exhibition Corporation Act world exhibition. All this bill seeks to do is to restrict the manner in which the corporation spend this grant; the governor in council is now asking parliament to restrict the corporation a little further in what it can do with the money.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: We seem to be spending a lot of time discussing a point of order-a point of order which certainly seems to have some basis-and I wonder whether the minister would not consider withdrawing his motion, starting again and putting a resolution on the order paper.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: I think we had better hear from the Chair, first.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: I am trying to avoid, if possible, a ruling from the Chair and the chance of a division.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
We will accept the ruling
of the Chair.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Would the Secretary of State explain his use of language when he says that what is being asked is a restriction on the powers of the corporation or of the governor in council? Let me stick to this one point. The legislation as enacted last December says, in section 5(1) that the commissioner general and the deputy commissioner general "shall each be paid by the corporation such salaries as are fixed by the governor in council." The proposal is to amend that, so as to make it read "such salaries and allowances as are fixed by the governor in council". It seems to me that this is not restrictive. It seems to me that this is enlarging the way in which this money can be spent.
I could take up other aspects of the bill, for example, the enlarging of the area where the fair could be held. The geographical limits set out in the original act were much more restricted than those proposed in this bill. As I say, I find it hard to understand the language used by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). If the bill, were, in fact, restricting the objects on which the money could be spent I would have no point of order, but it is precisely because the bill has brought in at least one new purpose which was not there before, that I think section 54 of the British North America Act comes into play.
In one of the citations which I read-I think it was citation 243-it says further down in the paragraph that if a bill such as the present bill gets into committee and the approval of the governor general has not been given in advance, it can be given at that time. I am not holding out for the suggestion made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) that we should start over again, by having a resolution, if

Business of the House this could be dealt with in another way; but having in mind the express provision of the British North America Act in this regard it seems to me we should be careful. I can see someone coming along later and saying these allowances were paid illegally and we would have another field day for the lawyers.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: Let us hear from Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if it would not be more conducive to good order and progress in the house if we were to let this matter stand and go on with the next item of business. There would, as I understand it, be no delay if the government decided to introduce a resolution to precede the bill; it would not kill the bill in any way. I am not suggesting that if a ruling were made by the Chair it would necessarily be in favour of the point of order advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but since time is advancing this evening it is the opinion of the Chair that the matter might be allowed to stand until tomorrow and the next order of business called.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was just rising to make the same suggestion to Your Honour. It was obviously a very debatable point we were discussing-a matter which only the Chair can decide. I may say at once the government is only too happy to abide by whatever decision the Chair may make in this matter but I think it would be helpful if we could, as you suggest, have this matter adjourned until the Speaker has had an opportunity to reflect upon it, and proceed to the next item of business.
Perhaps, while I am on my feet, you would permit me to inquire whether it might be the wish of the house to let us go on for half an hour so that we could hear the hon. lady give her exposition of the important measure which is the next order of business.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SITE, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is snowing outside now. We do not want any more of it.
On motion of Mr. Pickersgill the debate was adjourned.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.

speechtext:
On the order:
Second reading of Bill C-125, an act to amend the Old Age Assistance Act, the Disabled Persons Act and the Blind Persons Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Before the hon. lady makes her comments with respect to this bill I think

we would do well to reflect on the suggestion made by the Secretary of State that we should sit half an hour beyond the normal sitting time in order that the hon. lady, or another minister, might make remarks of an introductory nature. Perhaps before we reflect on that suggestion we might consider it to be ten o'clock. This would give the hon. lady a fresh start tomorrow.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: Well, I suppose one bows to the inevitable.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Has anyone called it ten o'clock?
We are prepared to go on for half an hour.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: I thought I had made it clear earlier that it should be ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: It is not ten o'clock yet.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING OLD AGE ASSISTANCE, BLIND AND DISABLED PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: Thirty seconds to go.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If it is now ten o'clock, may I ask what is to be the business for tomorrow and Wednesday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think, in line with the suggestion made by Your Honour, it would be preferable to go ahead now with the bill on the pensions and then, perhaps, after that Your Honour could give a decision on the point which was raised and we would go ahead with the bill on the world's fair.
Then we would proceed to deal with the other two bills which were indicated by my colleague the Solicitor General, the measure concerning the auditors of the C.N.R. and the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act. If these were to be completed I am sure, by consultation, we could get something more done tomorrow.
I am very grateful for the excellent cooperation there has been today and if we can get at least those four measures done tomorrow I think we can be much more hopeful about the conclusion of the session.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What are the prospects for Wednesday-legislation or estimates?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think we should take estimates on Wednesday, and I hope to confer with hon. gentlemen opposite about which estimates will be taken. I would hope that on Wednesday the house would agree to sit either in the evening or, if that does not seem possible, at least until seven o'clock so as to make some progress with whatever estimates are before us.
It being one minute after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
Tuesday, December 10, 1963
